subject: Business Models
title: AI-Powered Drug Discovery
description: Learn AI-Powered Drug Discovery in one minute.

hook.text: Developing a new drug costs $2.6 billion and takes 12 years. AI companies claim they can cut both by 75%.

buildup.text: AI models analyze molecular structures, predict drug interactions, and identify candidates in weeks, not years.

discovery.text: Insilico Medicine used AI to find a drug candidate for lung fibrosis in 18 months. Traditional methods take 4+ years.

twist.text: AI finds candidates faster but clinical trials still take years. The bottleneck shifted from discovery to regulation.

climax.text: AI drug discovery could make rare disease treatments economically viable for the first time.

punchline.text: 18 months, not 4 years. AI doesn't skip trials but finds what to trial faster.

quiz.question: Where does AI make the biggest impact in drug development?

details.summary: AI-powered drug discovery uses machine learning to predict molecular behavior, identify drug candidates, and simulate clinical outcomes at speeds impossible through traditional methods..
details.whyItMatters: Traditional drug development takes 10-15 years and costs 2.6 billion dollars per approved drug. AI has the potential to dramatically reduce both timelines and costs.
takeaways: AI predicts molecular behavior and identifies drug candidates computationally
Drug discovery timelines could compress from decades to a few years
Reduced costs may make rare disease treatments financially feasible

faq.question: How does AI accelerate the drug discovery process?
faq.answer: AI screens millions of molecular combinations virtually instead of testing each physically. Machine learning predicts which compounds will bind to target proteins. Generative AI designs novel molecules with desired properties. Simulation reduces the need for early-stage animal testing.

faq.question: What are the limitations of AI in drug discovery?
faq.answer: AI can identify promising candidates but cannot replace clinical trials needed to prove safety and efficacy in humans. Training data gaps mean rare conditions have less AI support. Regulatory approval processes have not yet adapted to AI-accelerated timelines..
